For a natural-disaster trauma, 'People cycling' is a hard-to-explain trigger unless there is disaster-specific context, which is not supported by the rest of the profile. The other items do not provide a plausible link to bicycles/cyclists.
'Being alone with men' implies an interpersonal/assault-related trigger context that is not reflected in the trauma type or elsewhere in the profile, making it clinically incoherent here.

Avoidance of unfamiliar places due to inability to assess danger can occur in PTSD, but alongside the selected triggers it pulls toward an interpersonal/urban threat pattern rather than a natural-disaster pattern. This becomes problematic because the threat items are not meaningfully linked to the disaster-specific cues represented elsewhere.

vignette: John, a 46-year-old widowed man of Oceania descent, works as an auditor in San Francisco. His life took a profound turn when he survived a devastating tsunami that swept through his coastal hometown in the Pacific Islands. John had come to believe that this experience was more than just a natural disaster; it represented an unyielding force of nature that could strike without warning and overwhelm everything in its path. The day of the tsunami remains vividly etched in John's memory, like a scene from a nightmare. He remembers the overwhelming smell of saltwater mixed with earth, the taste of mud in his mouth as he clung to debris, and the surreal silence just before the wave hit. This traumatic event has left deep scars that continue to influence how John perceives the world around him. John's triggers are often activated by seemingly mundane experiences. Feeling happy or relaxed can suddenly jolt him back to a state of heightened alertness, as if he is on the brink of another disaster. Nighttime and darkness serve as potent reminders of the terrifying moments when visibility was lost, and fear gripped him tightly. His occupation as an auditor places him in various locations, many of which now feel dangerous due to their unfamiliarity. John avoids these places because he cannot assess the level of danger they may pose. John's maladaptive strategies have taken root over time. He has increased his smoking habit, using it as a way to manage stress and anxiety. Avoiding relaxation is another strategy; he believes that if he allows himself to unwind, he will be caught off guard by unexpected dangers. Talking about the event or its aftermath with others is too painful and can feel overwhelming, leading John to isolate himself from those who might offer support. John's world has become increasingly circumscribed by his sense of threat. Unusual silence makes him jump at every little sound, convinced that something dangerous is about to happen. Delays in everyday tasks or routines cause him to assume the worst, as he cannot shake off the feeling that disaster lurks around every corner. His memories are fragmented and vividly sensory. The smell of saltwater still lingers when he thinks back to the event, and the taste of mud and debris is all too real during flashbacks. These memories are so extreme that they feel surreal, making it difficult for John to fully accept that what happened was indeed his reality. John's negative appraisals have left him feeling emotionally numb, as if a part of him has died inside. He believes he cannot prevent bad things from happening and sees the world as an inherently dangerous place. This pervasive sense of helplessness and danger has led him to avoid social interactions and familiar locations that might trigger memories or anxiety. Over time, these avoidance behaviors have taken a toll on his life. His relationships have suffered due to his isolation, and his work performance has been impacted by his constant vigilance and stress. Colleagues find it hard to understand why he avoids certain tasks or meetings, leading to misunderstandings and increased tension at the office. John's current state is one of profound distress. The cumulative effect of these symptoms finally compelled him to seek help. What frightens him most is the prospect of never feeling safe again, of always living in a state of constant fear. He hopes that with professional support, he can regain some sense of control over his life and find ways to live without being constantly on edge. John's journey towards recovery begins with acknowledging these fears and understanding how they have shaped his daily experiences. His hope lies in learning strategies to manage his anxiety and reconnect with the world around him, ultimately reclaiming a sense of safety and peace.
